title: Developer migration guide: sync-to-incremental-streaming-with-tools
body:
Context:
This is a working PRD-style guide aimed at product + developer-experience teams to design the recommended path for customers and internal SDKs to migrate from single-response (synchronous) Hosted API usage to an incremental streaming model that supports tool-calls and structured, commit-aware partial outputs.

Why this doc exists (problem statement):
- Many customers today call the Hosted API in a synchronous model: send prompt, receive final response. This works for lightweight generative tasks but fails for complex tool orchestration, large outputs (long documents), and mobile/edge clients with fragile networks.
- Streaming reduces perceived latency and enables progressive UX, but it introduces complexity: partial/invalid JSON, tool-call handshakes mid-stream, client-side reconciliation, and SDK ergonomics for idempotency and resume.
- We need a pragmatic, backward-compatible migration path that:
  * Minimizes server-side breaking changes,
  * Provides clear SDK patterns for JavaScript/Python/Go,
  * Makes structured output and tool transactions reliable at scale.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Customers can switch a route from sync to incremental streaming without reauthorizing tokens or changing app-level contracts in most cases.
- SDKs provide clear abstractions that reduce app-level glue code for: partial JSON assembly, tool-call handshake, commit/abort semantics, and resume after interruption.
- Observability surfaces that show token-level latency, incomplete output rates, tool-call success/failures, and reconstruction errors.
- Migration checklist, examples, and compatibility flags for safe rollouts.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not prescribe low-level wire formats that are implementation-only (those live in runtime-protocol design).
- We will not attempt a one-size-fits-all streaming protocol for third-party tool plugins; we provide primitives and SDK helpers.

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want the initial chunk of model output to appear within 100–300ms for typical prompts so users see progress.
- As an SDK consumer, I want a simple callback/async iterator interface that yields either delta-text, structured frames, or tool-call events with clear call-to-action semantics.
- As an integrator, I want to call external services (tools) deterministically when the model requests them and be able to respond back into the session without losing context.
- As an SRE, I want telemetry on partial-output assembly errors and the percentage of resumed sessions that succeed.

High-level approach and principles:
- Backwards compatibility: default routes remain synchronous. Streaming is opt-in via a route flag and a well-documented Accept/Upgrade HTTP header or SDK client option.
- Primitive-first SDKs: SDKs expose low-level event streams (frames) and higher-level helpers (assembleJSON, toolHandshake). Customers can use helpers or handle raw frames.
- Commit semantics: introduce explicit commit points in the stream (commit-frame) that signal the server and SDK that a structured chunk is final and safe to index/store.
- Tool-call choreography: model can emit a tool_request frame with a stable request_id; SDK exposes an accept/execute/response API for that request_id. Responses are then fed back into the same session stream.
- Resume and idempotency: every streaming session has a session_id and monotonic sequence numbers for frames. SDKs should persist minimal state (last_seq, partial_buffer) to resume.

API surface (recommended):
- HTTP header toggle: X-Redwood-Stream: incremental (or q: streaming=true param).
- Response stream frames (newline-delimited JSON lines): three top-level "frame_type" values: delta, control, tool_request.
  * delta: {"frame_type":"delta","seq":123,"data":"text chunk or snippet","kind":"text|json-part|binary"}
  * control: {"frame_type":"control","seq":124,"control_type":"commit|checkpoint|error","payload":{...}}
  * tool_request: {"frame_type":"tool_request","seq":125,"request_id":"r-...","tool":"http_get","args":{"url":"..."},"schema_hint":{...}}
- Commit protocol: control.commit includes a stable logical cursor id and optional schema version. Once seen and acknowledged by client SDK, server may mark tokens as committed for billing/reporting semantics and snapshotting.
- Tool call lifecycle: model emits tool_request -> SDK exposes request object -> application executes tool -> app returns tool_result via SDK -> server injects tool_result into model context and resumes generation.

SDK ergonomics (JS/Python/Go patterns):
- Provide two layers: low-level stream API (async iterator or event emitter) + high-level composer (StreamSession).
- StreamSession responsibilities: frame ordering, partial JSON reassembly, commit acknowledgements, tool_request convenience helpers (auto-ack, manual mode), automatic low-overhead checkpointing to localStorage / disk for resume.
- Example JS surface (sketch):
  const session = client.openStream({route: 'chat:assistant', streaming: true});
  for await (const frame of session) {
    if (frame.frame_type === 'delta') session.append(frame);
    if (frame.frame_type === 'tool_request') {
      const {request_id, tool, args} = frame;
      // either session.autoExecute(tool, args) or let app respond
    }
    if (frame.frame_type === 'control' && frame.control_type === 'commit') session.ackCommit(frame.cursor);
  }

- High-level helpers: assembleStructuredJSON(frameStream) -> yields valid JSON objects as soon as committed; on partial JSON error, raise a StructuredAssemblyError with diagnostic info (seq ranges, raw chunks).

Structured output best practices:
- Encourage model to emit small atomic objects with explicit commit checkpoints rather than a single massive object. This makes partial consumption possible and reduces reconstruction errors.
- Support schema hints attached to frames so SDKs can validate incrementally. If schema validation fails at an assembly checkpoint, SDK surfaces clear diagnostics and optional auto-fallback heuristics (tolerate trailing commas, attempt heuristic joins).

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Broken partial JSON: SDK exposes automatic repair heuristics with opt-in flags; always surface original raw frames for auditing.
- Tool execution failures: SDK/application must return a standardized tool_error payload referencing request_id; model may choose to retry, fall back, or emit an abort control frame.
- Network interruption: session persists last_seq and partial_buffer; on resume, client requests frames after last_seq. Server must retain transient stream buffers for a configurable TTL (default 5 minutes).

Observability and telemetry:
- Emit metrics per-route: "percent_sessions_streaming", "partial_json_errors_per_1k_sessions", "tool_request_rate", "tool_request_success_rate", "resume_success_rate".
- Tracing: every frame includes an optional trace_id; tool_request includes request_id used as a span id.
- Logs: store raw frame digests (not full text) for first-party troubleshooting; make opt-in for enterprise privacy customers.

Rollout plan (staged):
- Phase 0: internal dogfood with SDKs and a "streaming-beta" route flag for a subset of internal teams.
- Phase 1: external alpha (select customers) with explicit feature flag. Provide migration docs and example apps.
- Phase 2: wider beta, add schema-hinting and checkpoint telemetry.
- Phase 3: GA with SLA notes, and a migration checklist in Console for route toggles.

Migration checklist for customers (developer-facing):
- Identify routes currently used synchronously and their expected response sizes.
- Add basic streaming test harness (client that can consume frames and assemble JSON).
- Switch one non-critical route to streaming behind a feature flag and instrument partial_json_errors.
- Implement tool_request handlers for any models that may request tools; prefer synchronous auto-exec for simple tools.
- Enable resume TTL and test reconnects under realistic network conditions.
- Plan for commit semantics: choose whether to index/store content only after commit frames.

Examples and small recipes (app patterns):
1) Mobile progressive preview: stream first N tokens as lightweight text deltas, present a progress placeholder while JSON object parts are assembled. Commit triggers UI replace with the full structured card.
2) Deterministic tool orchestration: model emits tool_request for entity enrichment; app executes enrichment synchronously and returns result. Server injects result and model continues with deterministic structure.

Open questions / decisions (early draft):
- Server retention TTL: 5 minutes vs 30 minutes tradeoff (memory and cost vs developer ergonomics).
- Billing semantics for partially streamed tokens before commit: should we bill as generated? Should commit mark persisted tokens for long-term retention?
- Schema hint expressiveness: lightweight JSON Schema subset vs custom compact schema.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Engineering: prototype sequence-numbered frame wire format and server-side buffer TTL (owner: Diego).
- SDK: implement JS/Python StreamSession prototype with assembleStructuredJSON and tool_request helpers (owner: Aisha).
- Product: prepare migration docs and Console route flag UI copy (owner: Renee).
- SRE: propose default buffer TTL and storage sizing for streaming buffers (owner: Samir).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic — we prefer incremental developer helpers over a heavyweight protocol that tries to solve every edge case.
- Please comment on the commit semantics (should commit be required to avoid partial indexing?) and resume TTL tradeoffs.

References / related work:
- CONFLUENCE-1234: streaming proto design notes
- Example app: github.com/redwood-inference/progressive-preview (WIP)

Appendix: short FAQ
Q: Can I keep existing sync clients working?
A: Yes — default behavior unchanged. Streaming is an opt-in route toggle; SDKs will continue to support sync call surfaces.
Q: How do I test tool calls locally?
A: SDK includes a local simulator that replays tool_request frames and accepts canned tool responses; see SDK example repo.
Q: What about security for tool calls?
A: Tool execution is in-app; model only emits tool_request semantics. App enforces auth/ACL for executing external calls.

End of draft.
